narrative:
Based on your academic and admissions profile, the model estimates a 59.8 percent probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. Because that risk is higher than the chance of passing, the law school decided to deny your application.

The single most influential factor in this decision was your class standing in your third year. You placed in the bottom tenth of your class, while students admitted to this program typically sat around the sixth decile. Being that far below the average academic performance was a strong signal pointing toward bar exam failure. The second most important factor was your family income. Interestingly, your lower-middle income background actually nudged the prediction in the opposite direction—toward passing—since students from that bracket in the dataset performed slightly better than expected. However, this positive influence was not strong enough to overcome your academic record. The third major factor was your LSAT score. At 24, your score is well below the average of about 37 among accepted students, and this also pushed the prediction firmly toward failure.

Given these results, the clearest path forward is to strengthen the two areas that counted against you. Consider retaking the LSAT after targeted preparation; a substantially higher score would directly reduce your predicted failure risk. In addition, if you have the opportunity to retake courses or improve your academic standing before reapplying, focus on raising your class percentile. A revised application with an LSAT score closer to the program average and a higher class rank would likely produce a much more favorable outcome.
